content: The transmission of Taenia solium infections, including taeniasis and cysticercosis, is closely linked to travel and tourism to endemic regions. The T. solium taeniasis/cysticercosis complex involves two distinct life stages and clinical manifestations in humans. Taeniasis, an intestinal infection caused by the adult tapeworm when humans act as the definitive host, typically results in low morbidity. However, it is the primary source of cysticercosis infections in both humans and pigs. Cysticercosis, on the other hand, occurs when humans act as intermediate hosts and are infected with the larval stage of the parasite (cysticercus). This condition is a significant global cause of seizure disorders, particularly in the form of neurocysticercosis (NCC), and also leads to economic losses due to infected pork (porcine cysticercosis). The prevalence of neurocysticercosis among individuals with seizure disorders is a reliable indicator of the disease burden. In some endemic areas of Latin America, NCC accounts for approximately 30% of all seizure disorders. Subarachnoid NCC is associated with complications such as intracranial hypertension and increased mortality. Control of Schistosoma japonicum and cestode infections in humans is further complicated by their zoonotic nature, as animals such as cattle, buffalo, rodents, dogs, sheep, and pigs can act as reservoirs for human transmission. Despite the proven efficacy of praziquantel (PZQ) in treating cestode infections and schistosomiasis, there is a pressing need for improved drugs, combination regimens, and optimized dosages to enhance treatment outcomes and reduce transmission risks. Research priorities for helminth infections, as outlined by the WHO Technical Report Series No. 972, emphasize the long-lasting nature of these infections, often involving multiple helminth species (a phenomenon known as polyparasitism). This co-occurrence is driven by shared ecological and environmental factors, infection routes, host susceptibility, and socioeconomic conditions. The global burden of human neurocysticercosis remains unknown, but efforts are underway to quantify its impact in endemic regions of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, as well as in industrialized countries like the USA, where immigration from endemic areas has led to an increase in cases. Robust estimates of the proportion of NCC among individuals with epilepsy, combined with epilepsy prevalence and incidence data, could help assess the disease burden in endemic areas. Studies have shown that individuals with multiple helminth infections often experience the most severe disease, suggesting that polyparasitism may exacerbate morbidity beyond the sum of single-species infections. Additionally, co-infections may increase susceptibility to other diseases, such as malaria or HIV, due to the immunosuppressive effects of helminth infections. Efforts to understand the interactions between co-existing parasites within the same host are critical for determining their effects on immune responses, resistance, susceptibility, and clinical outcomes. These findings are shifting prevention and control strategies from single-drug treatments to integrated approaches targeting multiple neglected tropical diseases, including onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, soil-transmitted helminthiases, and schistosomiasis. The Disease Reference Group on Helminth Infections (DRG4) has identified research priorities to address these challenges, focusing on interventions, epidemiology, surveillance, environmental and social ecology, data modeling, and basic biology. The group has prioritized research areas such as vaccine development, new drug discovery, diagnostic tools, and integrated control strategies. Stakeholder consultations and regional input have been integral to validating and refining these priorities. These efforts aim to break the cycle linking helminth infections to poverty, poor sanitation, and marginalization, ultimately supporting the control and elimination of these diseases.
